raw_case_text: A 6-year-old male patient presented with epigastric pain and abdominal distension for 10 days. For the last 2 days, he developed severity of epigastric pain increases along with increase in abdominal distension. However, history of trauma was absent. On general examination, patient's general condition was poor with pulse rate of 120/min and blood pressure of 80/54 mmHg. Abdominal examination revealed abdominal distension with mild tenderness. His plain X-ray abdomen erect view showed ground-glass appearance and USG was suggestive of the moderate peritoneal collection. Laboratory investigations showed Hemoglobin 8.8 g/dl, total leukocyte count - 18,500/mm3, total bilirubin 3.22 mg/dl (indirect 1.02 mg/dl), alkaline phosphatase 826.5 IU/L, alanine aminotransferase 262 IU/L, and aspartate aminotransferase 490 IU/L, negative Widal test. After adequate hemodynamic resuscitation, USG-guided diagnostic tap was performed which showed a bilious aspirate that was sent for biochemical examination. On biochemical examination, aspirated fluid confirmed as bile. The decision for laparotomy was taken and on exploration through supraumbilical midline vertical incision, about 1.5 L clear bile drained and whole bowel was found to be stained with bile pigments. Liver parenchyma and whole bowel were normal. Bile was coming out through a rent of 0.5 cm size at anterior surface of CHD just above the commissure. Gallbladder was thickened without any calculus and perforations [Figure 1]. After peritoneal lavage with lukewarm saline, biopsy was taken from margin of the rent. Common bile duct (CBD) also explored with no calculus or any impending perforation; distal patency was also checked. A 10-French T-tube was placed through the rent with the placement of subhepatic drain [Figure 2]. Postoperative period was uneventful. The patient was orally allowed on day 4. After 2 weeks, there was no subhepatic collection on USG and normal T-tube cholangiogram following which T-tube was removed [Figure 3]. Histopathology report showed normal fibrocollagenous tissue infiltrated by mild inflammatory infiltrate, no evidence of granuloma or malignancy. On follow-up after 6 months and 1 year, the patient is doing well.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 6-year-old boy presented with a 10-day history of epigastric pain and abdominal distension that markedly worsened over the preceding 2 days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient experienced epigastric pain and progressive abdominal distension for 10 days, with an acute increase in pain severity and distension during the 2 days prior to presentation.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for worsening epigastric pain and abdominal distension. Pertinent negative: no trauma.

objective.physical_examination: On admission, general condition was poor with tachycardia (pulse rate 120/min) and hypotension (blood pressure 80/54 mmHg). Abdominal examination revealed distension with mild diffuse tenderness.
objective.routine_investigations: Hemoglobin 8.8 g/dL, total leukocyte count 18,500/mm^3, total bilirubin 3.22 mg/dL (indirect 1.02 mg/dL), alkaline phosphatase 826.5 IU/L, ALT 262 IU/L, and AST 490 IU/L; Widal test was negative. Erect plain abdominal X-ray showed a ground-glass appearance, and abdominal ultrasonography demonstrated moderate free peritoneal fluid. Ultrasound-guided diagnostic paracentesis yielded bilious fluid, which was biochemically confirmed as bile.
objective.advanced_workup: Exploratory laparotomy via a supraumbilical midline vertical incision drained approximately 1.5 L of clear bile with diffuse bile staining of a structurally normal bowel and liver. A 0.5 cm spontaneous perforation (rent) was identified on the anterior wall of the common hepatic duct (CHD) just above the confluence/commissure, with a thickened acalculous gallbladder and a patent, stone-free common bile duct (CBD). Biopsy of the CHD perforation margin showed normal fibrocollagenous tissue with mild inflammatory infiltrate and no granuloma or malignancy.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Spontaneous perforation of the common hepatic duct (CHD) causing generalized biliary peritonitis, confirmed by bilious paracentesis, exploratory laparotomy (identifying a 0.5 cm anterior CHD rent), and benign ductal margin histopathology. Typhoid fever (negative Widal and normal bowel intraoperatively), choledocholithiasis, and malignancy were ruled out. Following hemodynamic resuscitation, the patient underwent peritoneal lavage, CBD exploration, placement of a 10-French T-tube through the CHD rent, and subhepatic drainage. Postoperative recovery was uneventful: oral intake resumed on day 4, follow-up ultrasound and T-tube cholangiogram at 2 weeks were normal (allowing T-tube removal), and the child remained completely well at 6-month and 1-year follow-up.
